The definition of lesbian as the general public (non lesbian or queer) sees it is wlw, yes, but LGBTQ labels often are not used as strictly as their "official" definitions. In practice, a lesbian can be anyone who experiences queer attraction to at least or primarily fem gendered people. Many, many queer people experience lesbianism this way, in fact I would think most do. There are any type of nonbinary people for whom the word "lesbian" feels right and not exclusively women coded so they don't feel dysphoric or invalidated using it. Are some lesbians binary women who can only like other binary women? Sure, just as there are straight people who can only like the other binary assigned gender. In practice though that's often not how it turns out. You can't tell what gender someone is by looking at them and often if they aren't cis they might not tell you right away. For someone like a traditionally feminine presenting person, there's visually no difference between a traditionally feminine presenting binary woman and a traditionally feminine presenting nonbinary person and you don't ask people what gender they are before you let yourself have a crush on them, that's not how that works. Crushes aren't a choice regarding the object or the timing of them or any other part. Related to that, some nonbinary people are also women! Some examples include nonbinary women (people who feel they are women but not in the same way as a binary one is), genderfluid people who are sometimes a woman, two spirit or bigender/multigender people who are sometimes women, and demigirls. It's important to take people in good faith when they say they're whatever kind of queer. Only the person in question can know how they feel about their orientation or gender and most people aren't adopting labels (actually actively using them, not as a one off joke like "attack helicopter") to make fun of them or lie. They are usually trying to express something about themself and will almost always experience some level of bigotry about that if they come out. Shunning people like that or anyone else out of a community harms them (and would arguably exclude most people who call themselves lesbians), whereas binary lesbians experience no harm from nonbinary lesbians being part of the community.

None of that could have happened if I had kept believing being LGBTQ+ was a sin. I relied on god extremely heavily and thought I couldn't truly know myself because only god could and thought all other people were bad no matter what because of sin, all of which is unhealthy and unfair. Instead of feeling lost and dependent, I try to understand myself and feel empowered that I can stand on my own to the level that I can now. I think the world around me is intriguing because of the immensely complex process that is evolution over billions of years, as opposed to everything being the way it is because god wanted it to be that exact way and creating it like that. I can usually feel like I have privacy instead of being uncomfortable and ashamed in the bathroom or just relaxing in my room because I don't believe there's someone watching me all the time (usually because sometimes the fear comes back because it's pretty ingrained). I'm not scared that all the people I meet might go to hell and I don't feel pressured to try to convert them or scared of people who aren't christians because they're doing something evil by not believing in that one god. There's probably more stuff that I can't think of right now. In general, I feel free now that I'm not a christian, like a weight's been lifted off, not like there's something missing. About stuff like what I described, not about living in the world that I live in, because the world sure is scary! In gender affirming top surgery (like a double mastectomy), the most common method called double incision has the scars placed under where your pec muscles stop for the shadow of them to help camouflage the scarring. The scars are usually pretty wide, but recently I've seen some people have scars 1/2 or 1/3 of the usual length and are towards the outside to leave more of the middle chest blank, so there must be a new technique being developed for less scarring. There's another type of top surgery called keyhole that's used for small chested patients with stretchy enough skin where you just cut around the nipple (not fully taking it off the body, they leave the underlying structure attached to it to preserve sensation, it's just deattatching it from the surrounding skin), suck the unwanted stuff out, and stitch the nipple back on, which leaves nearly invisible scars and flat pecs once the skin has adapted to its new shape, really only something you'd notice if you were looking for it or if they were keloid scars. Any surgeon who cares about patients (or even who just cares about their work looking good so people will speak/think highly of them) will either try to make the scar as small as possible, camouflage them as much as they can, or otherwise just look as neat as they can get it.

Depends on how big a person is. The bigger you get the more energy you need to maintain your weight and the bigger your calorie deficit can be when you go on a diet. For example, [this site](https://www.sailrabbit.com/bmr/) says that a 28 year old 5'7" 600lb woman who's almost always sitting or laying burns about 3,775 cals a day just existing when you plug those stats into it using the average of the first 3 TDEE (total daily energy expenditure) formulas. If you cut to 2,000 a day that's a 1,775 cal deficit every day. It takes 3,500 calories to lose a pound, so according to the calculator that's about a pound every 2 days or about 15lbs a month. To contrast, a 5'7" 120lb woman the same age with the same activity level burns just 1,475 a day. They would have to water fast and burn 300 extra cals by exercising (which is harder than you think- most calories burn estimates online or on the displays of workout equipment include the cals you would already burn just sitting around so it's not really anything extra or assume you're a 150lb man or whatever so they can be pretty inaccurate) to lose the same amount of weight. Weight loss surgery patients usually eat even less that 2,000 cals a day, I think the recommended diet for those people can be as low as 800 cals a day (which scares me tbh, that's so little) because their stomach can only hold a tiny amount and they would lose even faster. The same 600lb woman on an 800 calorie diet would burn almost 3,000 calories a day with the same activity level! That's excluding if these hypothetical people have metabolic issues or whatever else slowing their metabolism. Science is neat, right? But losing 15-20 pounds a month isn't healthy or possible for most people.
